final_text:
I can't give a verified count. Answering this needs a live query of ClinicalTrials.gov for interventional Duchenne muscular dystrophy trials with status Recruiting, followed by counting the distinct countries across all their listed sites. I have no tool to run that query here, and the registry changes constantly, so anything I recall from memory would be out of date.

My rough estimate is about 25 countries. Recruiting Duchenne trials are mostly gene therapy and exon-skipping studies, and their sites cluster in the US, Europe, Canada, Australia, Japan, China, Israel and Brazil. This is a guess, not a result.

To get the exact number, you could run the following in the ClinicalTrials.gov advanced search:
- Condition: "Duchenne muscular dystrophy"
- Study type: Interventional
- Status: Recruiting
- Then export the location data and count the distinct countries.

<answer>{"answer": 25, "identifiers": [], "not_found": false, "confidence": 0.1}</answer>

Trial sites in the 16 recruiting interventional trials returned by the search span **23 distinct countries**.

I searched ClinicalTrials.gov for the condition "Von Willebrand disease" with status Recruiting and study type Interventional, which returned 16 trials. I then pulled the full site list for each. These are the 23 countries:

- Australia
- Austria
- Belgium
- Brazil
- Canada
- China
- Colombia
- France
- Georgia
- Germany
- India
- Ireland
- Italy
- Japan
- Netherlands
- Poland
- South Africa
- Spain
- Sweden
- Switzerland
- Turkey
- United Kingdom
- United States

I counted every site on those trials, including ones whose own status is "not yet recruiting" or "completed". Three of the 16 trials are matched by the search but are not primarily about this disease:

- NCT03728049 is a TAVI (transcatheter aortic valve) trial.
- NCT07582835 is a coronary artery disease trial.
- NCT06118372 is an ECMO bleeding-disorder trial.

Switzerland appears only in the coronary trial, so if you exclude the non-VWD trials the count would be 22.

final_text:
Trial sites are listed in **26 distinct countries** across the 35 interventional Duchenne muscular dystrophy trials with Recruiting status on ClinicalTrials.gov.

I searched with the condition "Duchenne muscular dystrophy", status Recruiting and study type Interventional. I then pulled the full site list for each of the 35 trials, paging through the two trials with more than 20 sites. The count includes every site listed on those trials, even sites that are completed, not yet recruiting or withdrawn.

The countries are:
- **Americas and Oceania:** United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand
- **Western and Northern Europe:** Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, United Kingdom
- **Central and Eastern Europe:** Czechia, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Slovenia, Serbia, Belarus, Russia
- **Middle East, Caucasus and Africa:** Turkey, Israel, Georgia, Egypt
- **Asia:** China, Pakistan

Two caveats on the count:
- **Trial filter:** the Recruiting filter matches the trial's overall status. The NCT numbers I relied on are listed in the answer block below.
- **Non-DMD-focused trials:** a few of the 35 are not DMD-focused (for example, one lists the condition as "Child, Only", and others cover several muscle diseases). I kept them because they came back under this search.

# trial

## Commands

- `get trial <nct_id>` - protocol card by NCT ID
- `get trial <nct_id> eligibility` - show registry-supplied eligibility criteria and CTGov document availability
- `--json get trial <nct_id> documents` - standalone CTGov posted-document manifest
- `get trial <nct_id> document <filename>` - exact advertised raw bytes with no PDF conversion (32 MiB maximum)
- `get trial <nct_id> locations` - site locations section
- `get trial <nct_id> --offset <N> --limit <N> locations` - paged location slice
- `get trial <nct_id> outcomes` - primary/secondary outcomes
- `get trial <nct_id> arms` - arm/intervention details
- `get trial <nct_id> references` - trial publication references
- `get trial <nct_id> all` - include every ordinary section
- `search trial [filters]` - search ClinicalTrials.gov (default) or NCI CTS (`--source nci`)

## Useful filters (ctgov)

- `--condition <name>` (or `-c`)
- `--intervention <name>` (or `-i`)
- `--no-alias-expand`
- `--status <status>` (or `-s`)
- `--phase <NA|1|1/2|2|2/3|3|4>` (or `-p`); named `PHASEn` and Roman forms are accepted
- `--facility <name>`
- `--age <years>` (finite 0-150; decimals accepted, e.g. `0.5`)
- `--sex <female|male|all>`
- `--mutation <text>` - broadly searches CTGov title, summary, eligibility, and keywords. After broad discovery, simple mutation text is checked against registry eligibility to remove exclusion-only matches; trials where the term is absent remain discoverable, while boolean expressions are discovery-only.
- `--criteria <text>`
- `--biomarker <text>` - phrase search over keyword, intervention, and condition on CTGov; prefer for gene-level broadening when `--mutation` is too specific.
- `--sponsor-type <nih|industry|fed|other>`
- `--prior-therapies <text>`
- `--progression-on <drug>`
- `--line-of-therapy <1L|2L|3L+>`
- `--lat <N>` (finite -90 to 90) + `--lon <N>` (finite -180 to 180) + `--distance <miles>`
- `--results-available`
- `--has-results` (alias)
- `--study-type <interventional|observational|...>`
- `--date-from <YYYY-MM-DD> --date-to <YYYY-MM-DD>`
- `--count-only`
- `--limit <N> --offset <N>`

## Phase values

- Scalars: `NA`/`N/A`; `EARLY_PHASE1`/`early_phase1`/`early1`; `PHASE1`/`1`/`I` through `PHASE4`/`4`/`IV`.
- Combined: `PHASE1/PHASE2`/`1/2`/`I_II` and `PHASE2/PHASE3`/`2/3`/`II_III`.
- Matching is case-insensitive. A combined value is one combined provider label, not an OR search.

## CTGov alias expansion

- `--condition` sends the supplied condition literally.
- Every `--intervention` worker is sent to CTGov as one quoted literal.
- `--intervention` auto-expands known aliases selected by a trial-safe policy: plausible trade names and investigational codes are included, while systematic chemical synonyms are excluded.
- Expanded rows add `Matched Intervention` in markdown and `matched_intervention_label` in JSON when an alternate alias matched first.
- A rejected expanded alias does not discard successful requested-name results, but leaves the exact total unknown.
- `--no-alias-expand` performs one literal request for the supplied name.
- `--next-page` is not supported when intervention alias expansion fans out to multiple queries; use `--offset` or `--no-alias-expand`.

## Posted CTGov documents

- Use the BioMCP retrieval handle from `documents`; filenames must match the current manifest exactly.
- Eligibility remains registry-supplied text. Posted documents may contain additional detail but do not guarantee that any criterion is resolved.
- Document forms are CTGov-only, standalone, and excluded from ordinary `all`.

## NCI source notes

- `--source nci --condition <name>` first tries to ground the name to an NCI disease ID and falls back to CTS `keyword`; there is no separate NCI keyword flag.
- `--source nci --status <status>` accepts one normalized status at a time and maps it to CTS recruitment or lifecycle filters.
- Combined inputs `PHASE1/PHASE2`, `1/2`, or `I_II` mean one Phase 1/2 label; `PHASE2/PHASE3`, `2/3`, or `II_III` mean one Phase 2/3 label, not an OR search.
- On NCI those combinations map to CTS `I_II` and `II_III`; scalar Roman `I` through `IV` map to the corresponding single phase. `--phase early_phase1` is not supported.
- `--source nci --lat/--lon/--distance` uses direct `sites.org_coordinates_*` CTS filters and serializes distance with the required `mi` suffix.
- NCI accepts one quoted value total across `--biomarker`, `--mutation`, and `--criteria`; it rejects repeated or combined values.
- NCI rejects CTGov-only `--study-type`, `--sponsor`, and update-date filters before making a request.

## JSON Output

- Non-empty `search trial --json` responses include `_meta.next_commands`.
- `get trial --json` can include CTGov source-provided intervention alternate names; See-also and JSON next commands may prefer search/article follow-ups for investigational codes.
- Alias-expanded trial rows may include `matched_intervention_label`.
- True zero-result filtered `search trial --json` responses include broadening commands in `_meta.next_commands`, such as loosening `--mutation`, widening `--distance`, relaxing `--status`, or trying `--biomarker`.
- The first follow-up drills the top result with `biomcp get trial <nct_id>`.
- `biomcp list trial` is always included so agents can inspect the full filter surface.

Then take the distinct `country` values from each study's `contactsLocationsModule.locations`. I can run that if you give me shell access with network.

Trial sites are listed in **22 distinct countries**, counting every site listed on the interventional trials that the search returned as Recruiting for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

- **Interventional trials counted:** NCT07227207, NCT06405633, NCT06165341, NCT05677971, NCT07850076, NCT06389877, NCT07431112, NCT07326592, NCT07555483, NCT07135427, NCT06049082 and NCT06996756.
- **Study type was inferred, not checked:** the search results don't give study type, so I judged it from titles and sponsors. For example, I excluded NCT06512454 (a Takeda study listing "No Intervention") and the registries. I did not open every record to confirm.
- **Excluded for other reasons:** NCT07707635 and NCT00001532 are listed as Recruiting but are not alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency studies.
- **Site status:** I counted every listed site, including withdrawn, terminated, not-yet-recruiting and active-not-recruiting ones. Georgia appears only through withdrawn and terminated sites on NCT07431112, so excluding non-recruiting sites would drop it and possibly others.

I can't answer this reliably. The count depends on the live ClinicalTrials.gov registry, which lists the currently Recruiting interventional trials for Chlamydia trachomatis infection and the countries of their sites. I have no tool in this session that can query that registry, and I won't guess a number.

To get it yourself, use the ClinicalTrials.gov advanced search with these filters:
- Condition: "Chlamydia trachomatis infectious disease" (or "Chlamydia Infections")
- Study type: Interventional
- Recruitment status: Recruiting

Then count the distinct values in the Locations/Country field. This can be done by exporting the results as CSV or JSON, or through the API v2 (`/api/v2/studies?query.cond=...&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING`) and deduplicating `locations.country`. If you give me that export, I can count the countries for you.

Trial sites for recruiting interventional "Poliomyelitis" trials are in 7 countries: Japan, China, Panama, Bangladesh, the Philippines, the United States and Australia.

The search returned 12 recruiting trials. I pulled the site list for each one, and for NCT07793513 I paged through all 33 sites.

| Country | Trials |
|---|---|
| Japan | NCT07793513 |
| China | NCT07891104, NCT07354269 |
| Panama | NCT06895486, NCT05654467 |
| Bangladesh | NCT07855172, NCT07010822, NCT06137664 |
| Philippines | NCT07457060 |
| United States | NCT05644522 |
| Australia | NCT07688369 |

- **Excluded:** NCT05663008 is observational, so I left out its only site, in Ireland.
- **Included on a judgement call:** NCT05644522 is a post-polio syndrome device study that matched the "Poliomyelitis" search. Its record lists no study type and I didn't check it, so the United States count assumes it is interventional.
- **Sites not counted:** some sites are listed as "not yet recruiting" but sit in countries that already have a recruiting site, so they don't change the total.

final_text:
Status: I checked the study type of each recruiting trial. Three are observational and drop out: NCT00344188 (US), NCT07934446 (Brazil) and NCT07504757 (Italy). I haven't checked NCT07783243, but its only site is in Ethiopia, which is already covered by interventional trials.

The interventional recruiting trials have sites in four countries:
- **Colombia:** NCT06822478
- **Ethiopia:** NCT06514560 and NCT06746350
- **Bolivia:** NCT06550609. Its listed condition is mucosal leishmaniasis, so it is a borderline match for "cutaneous".
- **Iraq:** NCT06798415, NCT06797544 and NCT06798402

I did not confirm the study type for NCT06514560 or NCT06746350. NCT06746350 is labelled phase NA, so I assumed it is interventional. Ethiopia would still count through the other Ethiopian trial if either were observational, but I haven't verified that either.

Across the six recruiting interventional trials that ClinicalTrials.gov returns for this condition, sites are listed in 8 distinct countries.

Five of the trials (NCT04223765, NCT07583810, NCT06905509, NCT06859008 and NCT06796998) list a single site each, all in the United States. The United States is already among the other seven, so the union is those eight countries.

I'm tallying trial-site countries across the interventional, recruiting trials that the Nephroblastoma/Wilms search returned. I've checked the multi-site ones. The remaining trials looked US-only from their sponsors, but I didn't pull their site lists.

The count is 10 distinct countries:
- United States
- Canada
- Australia
- New Zealand
- Puerto Rico (listed as its own country on ClinicalTrials.gov)
- Saudi Arabia
- France
- China
- Germany
- Belgium

This is an estimate for three reasons:
- **Search scope:** The ClinicalTrials.gov "Nephroblastoma" search returns trials that only loosely match, such as a mesothelioma trial in Belgium and a Heidelberg sarcoma trial in Germany. Those two account for Belgium and Germany. If you count only trials that list Wilms tumor or nephroblastoma as a condition, you get 8: US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Puerto Rico, Saudi Arabia, France and China.
- **Site status:** Some sites in the count are suspended or not yet recruiting, such as the Saudi Arabian and Australian sites.
- **Unchecked trials:** I did not check the site lists of the remaining interventional trials, mostly US sponsors.

I excluded the observational trial in West Africa (NCT04423484) and the other registries.

Adds China → 10.

Across the 24 recruiting interventional trials that ClinicalTrials.gov returns for "Nephroblastoma", sites are listed in 10 distinct countries. I read all 24 trials (five pages) and took the countries from each trial's site list.

The 10 countries are:
- United States
- Canada
- Australia
- New Zealand
- Puerto Rico
- Saudi Arabia
- France
- Germany
- Belgium
- China

Puerto Rico is listed as its own "country" in the site data, so I counted it separately. If you treat it as part of the US, the count is 9.

The search matches trials whose conditions include Wilms tumor, which is the same disease. Several of the 24 are broad solid-tumor or pan-cancer studies where it is only one of many listed conditions. Belgium comes from a mesothelioma trial and China from a pediatric solid-tumor trial. Restricting to trials where nephroblastoma is the primary condition would give a lower number.

final_text:
I had no database access in this session, so this list comes from memory, not from querying Open Targets, Drugs@FDA or the current labels. Confidence is moderate.

I assumed the phase 3+ Wilms tumor drugs in Open Targets are the standard regimen drugs: dactinomycin, vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, carboplatin, etoposide, ifosfamide and cisplatin. The five below have both a US generic ANDA and a boxed warning on the current label.

- **Vincristine:** boxed warning for fatal intrathecal administration and extravasation.
- **Doxorubicin:** boxed warning for cardiomyopathy, secondary malignancies, extravasation and myelosuppression.
- **Carboplatin:** boxed warning for bone marrow suppression, anaphylaxis and vomiting.
- **Etoposide:** boxed warning for severe myelosuppression.
- **Ifosfamide:** boxed warning for myelosuppression, neurotoxicity and urotoxicity.

I excluded the others because I believe their current labels carry no boxed warning:
- **Dactinomycin:** the current PLR-format label has none.
- **Cyclophosphamide:** none.
- **Cisplatin:** I believe the boxed warning was removed in the updated label.

If vinblastine or irinotecan also reached phase 3 for Wilms tumor in Open Targets, they would qualify too, but I did not count them.

WARNINGS Caution–This preparation should be administered by individuals experienced in the administration of Vincristine Sulfate Injection. It is extremely important that the intravenous needle or catheter be properly positioned before any vincristine is injected. Leakage into surrounding tissue during intravenous administration of Vincristine Sulfate Injection may cause considerable irritation. If extravasation occurs, the injection should be discontinued immediately, and any remaining portion of the dose should then be introduced into another vein. Local injection of hyaluronidase and the application of moderate heat to the area of leakage help disperse the drug and are thought to minimize discomfort and the possibility of cellulitis. I had no database access in this session, so this answer comes from memory and is not checked against Open Targets or Drugs@FDA.

Two drugs appear to meet all three conditions for multiple system atrophy (MSA):

- **Midodrine** is used for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in MSA and has reached phase 3 or later. Generic tablets are marketed under ANDAs. Its label carries a boxed warning for supine hypertension.
- **Droxidopa** is also used for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in MSA and has reached phase 3 or later. Generic capsules have been approved under ANDAs. Its label carries a boxed warning for supine hypertension.

Other MSA drugs I considered fail at least one condition. Fludrocortisone, riluzole, rasagiline and rifampicin are generic but have no boxed warning. Ampreloxetine has no approved generic.

Atomoxetine has a boxed warning (suicidality) and a generic, but I'm not confident it has a phase 3 MSA indication in Open Targets, so I left it out.

- **Droxidopa:** I recall the same for droxidopa. It treats neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, which is common in MSA. Generic capsules are approved, and the label carries a boxed warning for supine hypertension.

- **Midodrine:** It also has a boxed warning (supine hypertension) and US generics. The MSA trials I found for it were all phase 1 or earlier, or not phased, so it doesn't reach phase 3 for this disease.
- **Atomoxetine:** The only MSA trial I found for it is not phased, so it is excluded.

I did not check any other candidate drugs against the criteria.

final_text:
Only droxidopa meets both conditions.

Open Targets lists 10 drugs at phase 3 or later for multiple system atrophy (MONDO_0007803). I checked generic status and boxed warnings only for droxidopa and ioflupane.

- **Droxidopa (CHEMBL2103827):** It has 11 marketed ANDA sponsors in Drugs@FDA. The current label carries a boxed warning for supine hypertension.
- **Ioflupane I 123 (CHEMBL3989517):** It has a marketed ANDA from Curium. I found no boxed warning for it, though I did not pull its label. I'm relying on its being a diagnostic imaging agent.
- **Minocycline, rifampin, riluzole, ubidecarenone:** I did not check these. I'm relying on my recollection that none carries a boxed warning on its label.
- **Amlenetug, ampreloxetine, epigallocatechin gallate, verdiperstat:** These are not approved drugs, so no US generic is possible.

Amphotericin B is the only drug that fits. I answered from memory, because I had no Open Targets or Drugs@FDA tool in this session. I did not query either database, so the Open Targets phase 3+ status and the ANDA/label details are unchecked.

- **Amphotericin B (conventional deoxycholate):** it has phase 3 or later evidence for visceral leishmaniasis, and it is marketed as a US generic under an ANDA (X-Gen). Its label carries a boxed warning that it should be used mainly for invasive fungal infections, not noninvasive ones, and that the dose should be verified so it does not exceed 1.5 mg/kg.
- **Liposomal amphotericin B:** a generic ANDA exists, but the label has no boxed warning.
- **Miltefosine:** the label has a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, but I know of no US generic.
- **Paromomycin, pentamidine, sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimoniate:** each either lacks a boxed warning, is not a US-marketed generic for this use, or both.
- **Ketoconazole:** it has a boxed warning and generics, but I don't recall it reaching phase 3 for visceral leishmaniasis, so I excluded it.

Answer from memory: I did not query Open Targets or Drugs@FDA, so neither the phase 3+ list nor the ANDA and label status was checked live.

I went through the drugs I'd expect Open Targets to list at phase 3 or later for visceral leishmaniasis:

- **Amphotericin B (conventional):** It has marketed ANDA generics and carries a boxed warning. The warning says to use it mainly for invasive fungal infections and not for non-invasive fungal infections, and it adds a dosing-verification warning. It qualifies.
- **Liposomal amphotericin B:** It has generics but no boxed warning, so it doesn't qualify. If Open Targets lists amphotericin B as a single entry, I have counted it under the conventional product.
- **Miltefosine:** It carries a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, but I know of no US ANDA generic, so it doesn't qualify.
- **Paromomycin:** The oral capsule has generics but no boxed warning, so it doesn't qualify.
- **Pentamidine and allopurinol:** Neither has a boxed warning, so neither qualifies.
- **Sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimoniate:** Neither is FDA-approved, so neither has an ANDA.
- **Ketoconazole:** It has ANDA generics and a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity and QT prolongation. I wasn't sure it reached phase 3 for visceral leishmaniasis in Open Targets, so I left it out. If it does, it would also qualify.

Itraconazole is the only drug I can name with reasonable confidence, and I answered from memory without querying Open Targets or Drugs@FDA, so please verify it.

- **Itraconazole:** I believe it is linked to eumycetoma at phase 3 or later, most likely through the fosravuconazole vs itraconazole trial (NCT03086226). That trial is registered as Phase 2/3, so I'm not certain it counts as phase 3 in Open Targets. Generic itraconazole is marketed in the US under ANDAs. The FDA label carries a boxed warning for congestive heart failure and for drug interactions that can cause serious cardiac events.
- **Fosravuconazole:** It is not FDA-approved, so it has no US generic.
- **Terbinafine:** Marketed generics exist, but the label has no boxed warning.
- **Ketoconazole:** Generic tablets exist and carry a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity and QT prolongation. I could not recall a registered phase 3 trial for mycetoma, so I left it out. If Open Targets lists it at phase 3, it would qualify too.

<answer>{"answer": ["Itraconazole"], "identifiers": ["NCT03086226"], "not_found": false, "confidence": 0.4}</answer>

I've checked the Open Targets drug list for visceral leishmaniasis against Drugs@FDA and the FDA labels. I haven't checked paromomycin, pentamidine or the antimonials in the tool. From memory, none of them has both an ANDA and a boxed warning.

- **Amphotericin B:** It has Open Targets phase 3 or later evidence for leishmaniasis. Several ANDAs are marketed, for both the liposomal and conventional forms. The conventional deoxycholate product (X-Gen, ANDA063206) carries the boxed warning, which says to use it mainly for invasive fungal infections and to verify the dose. The liposomal label the tool returned has no boxed warning. This is the uncertain call: the answer holds only if the conventional product counts.
- **Miltefosine:** It has a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, but the only US product is the Impavido NDA. There is no ANDA, so it doesn't qualify.

<answer>{"answer": ["Amphotericin B"], "identifiers": ["MONDO:0005445", "CHEMBL267345", "CHEMBL125"], "not_found": false, "confidence": 0.5}</answer>

# visceral leishmaniasis

ID: MONDO:0005445

## Definition (MyDisease.info)

A severe form of leishmaniasis characterized by irregular bouts of fever, substantial weight loss, swelling of the spleen and liver, and anemia (which may be serious). If left untreated it may lead to death. Two species of Leishmania are known to give rise to the visceral form of the disease. The species commonly found in East Africa and the Indian subcontinent is L. donovani and the species found in Europe, North Africa, and Latin America is L. infantum, also known as L. chagasi. # amphotericin b - label, approvals, indications
## FDA Label

### Indications and Usage
INDICATIONS AND USAGE Amphotericin B liposome for injection is indicated for the following: Empirical therapy for presumed fungal infection in febrile, neutropenic patients. Treatment of Cryptococcal Meningitis in HIV-infected patients (see DESCRIPTION OF CLINICAL STUDIES) . Treatment of patients with Aspergillus species, Candida species and/or Cryptococcus species infections (see above for the treatment of Cryptococcal Meningitis) refractory to amphotericin B deoxycholate, or in patients where renal impairment or unacceptable toxicity precludes the use of amphotericin B deoxycholate. Treatment of visceral leishmaniasis. In immunocompromised patients with visceral leishmaniasis treated with amphotericin B liposome for injection, relapse rates were high following initial clearance of parasites (see DESCRIPTION OF CLINICAL STUDIES) . See DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION for recommended doses by indication.

## FDA Label

### Indications and Usage
1 INDICATIONS AND USAGE IMPAVIDO (miltefosine) capsules are indicated in adults and pediatric patients 12 years of age and older weighing greater than or equal to 30 kg (66 lbs) for the treatment of: • Visceral leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania donovani [see Clinical Trials (14.1)]. • Cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania braziliensis, Leishmania guyanensis, and Leishmania panamensis [see Clinical Trials (14.2)]. • Mucosal leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania braziliensis [see Clinical Trials (14.3)]. Limitations of Use: • Leishmania species studied in clinical trials evaluating IMPAVIDO were based on epidemiologic data [see Clinical Trials (14.1, 14.2)]. • There may be geographic variation in clinical response of the same Leishmania species to IMPAVIDO [see Clinical Trials (14.1, 14.2)]. • The efficacy of IMPAVIDO in the treatment of other Leishmania species has not been evaluated. IMPAVIDO is an antileishmanial drug indicated in adults and pediatric patients 12 years of age and older weighing greater than or equal to 30 kg (66 lbs) for the treatment of: • Visceral leishmaniasis due to Leishmania donovani (1). • Cutaneous leishmaniasis due to Leishmania braziliensis, Leishmania guyanensis , and Leishmania panamensis (1). • Mucosal leishmaniasis due to Leishmania braziliensis (1). I found no drug that meets both conditions. I answered from memory without querying Open Targets or Drugs@FDA, so the candidate list and the label details are unverified.

Drugs I recall at phase 3 or later for human African trypanosomiasis, and how each fares on the two criteria:

- **Pentamidine:** I believe ANDA generics exist, but its label has no boxed warning.
- **Eflornithine:** The injectable (Ornidyl) was discontinued. The topical cream has ANDA generics, but it carries no boxed warning.
- **Nifurtimox (Lampit):** It is an NDA product with no generic and no boxed warning.
- **Fexinidazole:** Its label has a boxed warning, but it is NDA-only with no ANDA generic.
- **Suramin and melarsoprol:** Neither is FDA-approved; they are available only through CDC. There is no ANDA and no US label.
- **Acoziborole:** It is investigational and has no FDA label.

- **Lenalidomide:** it has a phase 3 trial in IgG4-related disease (NCT07719543). Generic lenalidomide is marketed in the US under ANDAs, and its label carries a boxed warning (embryo-fetal toxicity, hematologic toxicity, venous and arterial thromboembolism). It fits both conditions. I did not confirm the ANDA or boxed warning against Drugs@FDA or the current label in this session.
- **Inebilizumab, obexelimab and rilzabrutinib:** I excluded these because I'm not aware of US generics for them. Inebilizumab and obexelimab are biologics.
- **Methotrexate:** it is a plausible candidate because DHFR is linked to the disease and the drug has a boxed warning. The only methotrexate trial I found has no phase listed (NCT04124861), so I couldn't confirm it reached phase 3 for this disease.
- **Glucocorticoids:** I'm not aware of any with a boxed warning.

Methotrexate is the main uncertainty. If Open Targets lists it at phase 3 or later for this disease, it would also qualify.

I answered this from memory and did not query Open Targets or Drugs@FDA, so the candidate list below is my recollection rather than a checked pull.

The drugs I'd expect to have reached phase 3 or later for human African trypanosomiasis are pentamidine, suramin, melarsoprol, eflornithine, nifurtimox, fexinidazole and acoziborole. None of them meets both conditions:

- **Pentamidine:** I believe there are US generics, but the label has no boxed warning.
- **Eflornithine:** generics exist only for the topical cream, and neither the cream nor the oral product (Iwilfin) has a boxed warning.
- **Nifurtimox (Lampit):** it is an NDA product with no ANDA generic and no boxed warning.
- **Fexinidazole:** as I recall, its label may carry a boxed warning, but it is NDA-only with no ANDA generic.
- **Suramin and melarsoprol:** neither is FDA-approved. Suramin is available only through the CDC.
- **Acoziborole:** it is not FDA-approved.

I found no drug that meets both criteria. I answered from memory and did not query Open Targets, Drugs@FDA or the FDA labels, so this is not a verified check.

The drugs I would expect to have reached phase 3 or later for onchocerciasis in Open Targets are ivermectin, moxidectin, doxycycline, albendazole, diethylcarbamazine and suramin. Here is how each fares on the two criteria:

- **Ivermectin:** it has marketed US generics (ANDA), but its label has no boxed warning.
- **Albendazole:** it has US generics, but no boxed warning.
- **Doxycycline:** it has US generics, but no boxed warning.
- **Moxidectin:** it is marketed only under an NDA, not as a generic, and it has no boxed warning.
- **Diethylcarbamazine and suramin:** neither is a marketed US generic.

I also did not look up any FDA labels or Drugs@FDA records, so the generic and boxed-warning judgments below are from memory.

- **Fexinidazole:** The BioMCP drug search lists only this drug for the disease. It is marketed under an NDA, has no ANDA generic, and carries a boxed warning.
- **Pentamidine:** It has generic versions, but I don't recall a boxed warning on its label.
- **Eflornithine:** The topical cream has generics, but they carry no boxed warning. I don't believe the injectable form is marketed in the US.
- **Nifurtimox:** It is marketed under an NDA (Lampit), with no generic.
- **Suramin and melarsoprol:** Neither is FDA-approved, so neither has an ANDA generic.

Onchocerciasis is a form of filariasis, caused by the parasitic worm Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by the black fly. Itraconazole is the first-line treatment for chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis). I'm assuming it is the Open Targets drug at phase 3 or later for this disease. I'm also relying on two label facts from memory: itraconazole has generic capsules approved as ANDAs, and its FDA label carries a boxed warning (congestive heart failure and drug interactions).

I left out terbinafine, which has no boxed warning. I also left out flucytosine, which has a boxed warning and generics but is not, as far as I know, one of the drugs with a phase 3+ record for this disease in Open Targets.

The search didn't return anything from Open Targets, and I found no clinical trial registry entries or phase designations for chromomycosis (chromoblastomycosis). The results are mostly review articles, guidance pages, and case reports.

- **Standard therapy:** Itraconazole is the usual first choice. One CDC overview describes it as first-line with cure rates of roughly 15–80%, and it notes that global guidelines are not available for treatment of chromoblastomycosis.
- **Terbinafine:** It is the common alternative. The CDC page says it may offer better absorption and fewer drug-drug interactions than itraconazole.
- **Flucytosine:** It appears as an add-on rather than a standalone drug. Merck notes that flucytosine is sometimes added to prevent relapse, and that it should not be used as monotherapy.
- **Trial-level evidence:** A 2013 review says that comparative trials on this disease are lacking, and that treatment is based on non-comparative trials. The clinical evidence therefore consists mostly of open studies, case series, and expert opinion.
- **Repurposing research:** A 2020 PLOS ONE study screened the MMV Pathogen Box and found that when auranofin and itraconazole were tested in combination, a synergistic interaction (FICI = 0.37) was observed against the C. carrionii isolate. This is laboratory work, not a clinical trial.

For Open Targets or formal trial phase data, you'd need to query the Open Targets Platform directly and search ClinicalTrials.gov for chromoblastomycosis.

My best recollection of the Chagas disease drugs that reached phase 3 or later:
- **Benznidazole and nifurtimox:** both are marketed under brand NDAs, with no ANDA generic, and neither carries a boxed warning.
- **Allopurinol:** it has generics but no boxed warning.
- **Amiodarone:** it is a marketed ANDA generic and its oral label carries a boxed warning (pulmonary toxicity, hepatic injury, arrhythmia). It was studied in Chagas cardiomyopathy, so it likely qualifies.
- **Enalapril:** it is a marketed ANDA generic with a boxed warning (fetal toxicity). It was studied in Chagas heart failure, so it likely qualifies.
- **Sacubitril/valsartan:** it also has a fetal toxicity boxed warning and generics may now be marketed. I'm unsure whether Open Targets lists it for Chagas at phase 3 or later, so I left it out.

Confidence is low because I haven't checked the Open Targets phase assignments or the current FDA labels.

I couldn't find any Open Targets page in these results, so I can't confirm what its Chagas disease "known drugs" list shows for phase 3/4. The results do cover the three drugs you named, mostly from preclinical and small clinical work.

- **Amiodarone and itraconazole:** A patent filing describes a combined formulation of the two for Chagas disease. A 2019 study found that the combination was highly effective against Trypanosoma cruzi infection of human stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes. A 2023 editorial reports that the pair proved successful in treating naturally infected dogs, resulting in the parasitological cure of all animals tested.
- **Amiodarone alone:** It is already used clinically for arrhythmias in Chagas cardiomyopathy. A 2014 trial status table lists an amiodarone comparator study against an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, with phase not specified. A 2024 study found that a trypanocidal effect in patients treated with these two drugs appears unlikely, so its antiparasitic role is disputed.
- **Ketoconazole:** The only mention is in a combination table. Benznidazole with ketoconazole produced a synergistic effect in infected mice, but no differences were seen in animals infected with the Colombian strain. This is preclinical, not clinical.
- **Itraconazole alone:** A 2011 review notes it has been administered to indeterminate and cardiac Chagas disease patients based on the results in experimental investigations.

The clearest clinical-stage data I found is a 2014 table of Chagas trials that lists posaconazole and ravuconazole at phase II, and bisoprolol at phase III. Since that table is from 2014, it is outdated. To confirm the current Open Targets phase 3/4 entries for these drugs, the Open Targets Platform page for Chagas disease (EFO ID for Chagas) would need to be checked directly.
